title: The Taj Mahal
hook: Shah Jahan's tomb for Mumtaz Mahal, framed with Qur'an verses

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mughals: Babur's homesick garden, Akbar's hall of debate. Your line was: he missed the melons. Did you plant anything where you are? Day nine hundred ninety-three.

Everything is in pairs. Walk through the great gate and the garden opens in front of you, split by a long channel of water that holds the white dome upside down. Minarets stand at each corner of the platform, matched. To the left of the tomb, a red sandstone mosque; to the right, a building that copies it exactly, so the view stays balanced. Inside, under the dome, two marble cenotaphs lie side by side. And that is where the balance breaks. One sits at the exact center. The other is pushed to the side, as if it arrived later and squeezed in. It did. Today: the Taj Mahal.
screen: `A DOME IN THE WATER.` → `EVERYTHING MATCHED.` → `ONE TOMB OFF-CENTER.`

segments.voice: The Taj Mahal was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife, the empress known by the title “Mumtaz Mahal”, who died while he was emperor. The center of the whole design belongs to her. When Shah Jahan himself died, he was laid beside her, and his tomb is the one off-center, breaking the balance. People call it a monument to love, and it is. But walk closer and the white marble is framed with writing. Black stone letters set into the marble, framing the arches and the gate: verses from the Qur'an. The calligrapher, Amanat Khan, signed his work, and the letters are said to grow larger as they climb, so that from the ground they look the same size all the way up. Among the verses on the great gate, guides point to the end of the surah called al-Fajr, the Dawn. In Pickthall's translation: "But ah! thou soul at peace! Return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure!" And then: enter among My servants, enter My garden. So a visitor walks through words about a soul returning to God, into a garden with water, toward a grave. The love story is real. But the building also speaks about death, judgment and paradise. The Taj holds two questions in white stone: how to honor the one you've lost, and where the soul goes next. A tomb for love.
screen: `A TOMB FOR AN EMPRESS.` · `SHAH JAHAN, OFF-CENTER.` · `LETTERS THAT GROW AS THEY CLIMB.` · `RETURN UNTO THY LORD.` · then, large: `A TOMB FOR LOVE.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember a love that's gone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you loved who has died, or a love that ended, or a person who moved far away. Let their face come. Let one ordinary memory come: a voice, a kitchen, a joke. You don't have to build anything. Just hold them for a minute, the way the garden holds the tomb at its center. If grief comes, let it. If you pray, you can pray for them, as Muslims pray for their dead. If you don't, simply say their name. The bell holds the time.
Mumtaz Mahal. The empress for whom Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in Agra, white marble framed with Qur'an verses about the soul returning to God. Today's word.
Your line: a tomb for love. Today, do one small thing to honor someone you've lost: say their name aloud, cook their dish, or tell someone a story about them. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Muslims pray for the dead and visit graves to remember them; the mosque beside the Taj Mahal is still used for Friday prayer.
